genxml.title: SHub 1 registers outside the I/O interface: interrupts, local block, real-time clock, PIO write status, TLB purge, junk bus LEDs
genxml.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
genxml.doc: SHub 1 offsets as the SGI Linux ia64 platform header defines them (SH1_ names), relative to the node's register space; the SHub 2 overlay changes them. Every register is 64 bits wide unless noted, because the kernel reaches all of them with 64-bit loads and stores. The header gives neither the unit a register belongs to nor reset values; the unit named in each doc is inferred from the register's name prefix and address block. Reset values are unknown except where the header's INIT macro names a value, which is recorded as inferred. Roles are paraphrased from the header comments and the kernel's use.

struct.name: CHIP_ID
struct.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffa0be1c (read) and 0xffa0f8c0 (storage of the fields); the compare against 17251 is site 0xffa959a6
struct.doc: Chip identification word at node offset 0x1_0000_0000 (memory and directory block by address); the name is ours. The PROM reads it through the node's global window at node start and stores bits 27:12 as the node's part number and bits 31:28 as its revision. The part number is compared with 17251 (0x4363) site 0xffa959a6, reached through a table, so that this word feeds the compare is inferred. A bounded read that returns the part number satisfies the PROM.

struct.name: MD_DQLP_DIR_PRIVILEGE_VECTOR
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: Memory and directory unit: privilege vector for access class 0 of the left directory queue port (header SH1_MD_DQLP_MMR_DIR_PRIVEC0, title 'privilege vector for acc=0'). Defined by the header; no use in any kernel file read. Layout and role unknown.

struct.name: MD_DQRP_DIR_PRIVILEGE_VECTOR
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: Same, right queue port (header SH1_MD_DQRP_MMR_DIR_PRIVEC0). The reading of DQLP and DQRP as left and right ports is inferred from the names.

struct.name: IPI_INT
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: Send an interprocessor interrupt (processor interface or local block, inferred). The sender writes this register in the target node's global MMR window with send set, the target's physical processor id, a delivery type, a vector and a fixed base. The kernel stores through uncached physical mode with release ordering, after a memory barrier. On a SHub 1 revision 2 or lower it holds a global lock around the store and waits for the PIO write status to drain.

struct.name: RTC_INT_CONFIG
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: Where the comparator interrupt of RTC 1, 2 and 3 is sent: type, target processor id, vector area and vector. The mmtimer driver writes the vector and processor id fields and leaves type, agent and base zero. The register has the same layout as the IPI message, without the send bit. A fourth comparator (RTC 0) exists; the driver comment says firmware uses it, and the header defines nothing for it.

struct.name: RTC_INT_ENABLE
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: Enable for the comparator interrupt of RTC 1, 2 and 3. The mmtimer driver disables it, sets the comparator to all ones, clears the pending bit, writes the configuration, enables, and only then writes the real expiry, in that order.

struct.name: EVENT_OCCURRED
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: Pending interrupt events for the node (SHub interrupt event occurred). The kernel's interrupt acknowledge reads it, keeps the bits in the mask of the junk-bus UART, IPI and the two II interrupts, and writes that value to the alias to clear them. Only bits the header names are recorded; the others are unknown.

struct.name: EVENT_OCCURRED_ALIAS
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: Clears pending events: the kernel writes the bits it wants cleared here and never reads it. That a one clears and a zero leaves a bit alone is inferred from the kernel writing back exactly the bits it read as set (interrupt acknowledge) and a single bit to clear one RTC event (the mmtimer driver). Neither the kernel nor the header says what a read returns.

struct.name: LB_REG_1002_0000
struct.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffc4e7f0 (offset and use); no Linux v5.3 name
struct.doc: Local block register, unnamed; the name is ours (address). SAL_A writes 0x15031010 to it on each of its two entries (reason 3 and reason 0). The image holds no other reference to the address, so it is never read back. The meaning of the value is unknown; a plain write-accepting register satisfies the PROM.

struct.name: LB_SLICE_REC
struct.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffa0e020 (read of the running processor's entry), 0xffc4e570 (reasons 1 and 2 only)
struct.doc: Per-slice local block record, 128 bytes apart (index = slice & 3); the name is ours. SAL_B reads the running processor's entry in the lock routine and writes its low byte as a progress code, so any value is accepted; SAL_A reads it into r31 for reasons 1 and 2 only. The meaning of the value is unknown.

struct.name: RTC_CTL
struct.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffa94d06, 0xffa94d26 (writes), 0xffa0da00 (read of the period); the SAL runtime component's chipset_rtc_period reads the same field
struct.doc: Real-time clock control; the name is ours. The PROM writes 0x100000000, then writes 0 to rtc, then writes 0x100000041, all at the SAL_B reset entry, before any read. The tick period in nanoseconds is 10 times (period + 1); with the PROM's write the field is 4, 50 ns, 20 MHz, which is also what SAL_FREQ_BASE for the real-time clock returns (1,000,000,000 divided by the period). The reset value never reaches the PROM. Roles of the other bits are inferred only. If a read returned 0 the PROM would assume a 10 ns period (100 MHz); every PROM deadline is in microseconds scaled by this period, so the counter must tick at the rate the field gives.

field.name: period
field.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffa0da00 and the SAL runtime's chipset_rtc_period

struct.name: IPI_ACCESS
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: Which processors may send interprocessor interrupts to this one (header title: CPU interrupt access permission bits). The only use found is the cross-partition driver reading it as the target of a protected remote read; the driver comment says there is no special reason for that choice. So the register can be read without harm; its bit layout and write behaviour are unknown. The SHub 1 PROM writes 1 here once, as the winner of the node election in SAL_A (SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffc4ea40); the meaning of 1 is unknown.

struct.name: SHUB_ID
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: SHub identification (local block, inferred). The kernel reads only the revision, to switch on its SHub 1.1 workarounds when it is 2 or lower, and in the fallback for an old PROM the nodes-per-bit field, which it reports as the region size. SHub 2's counterpart is not named in the header. The SHub 1 PROM also writes it (SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffa95a30, reached from 0xffa5f84c): it reads the word, replaces bits 42:32 with the node id, bits 45:44 with a size code and bits 52:48 with a nodes-per-bit code, and writes the word back; the other bits are stored as read, so they may be read only. After the write the three fields must read back as written. The first read, at main start, needs any node id in bits 42:32; the reset value is unknown. See prom-reset.md.

struct.name: PTC
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: Purge translation cache message, SHub 1 (header SH1_PTC_0 and SH1_PTC_1). To purge a virtual address range on every processor of a node the kernel writes the two registers of that node's global window back to back with interrupts and interruption collection off, the first with a type bit, the page-size exponent, the region id and a start bit, the second with the virtual address and a start bit; both stores are in one atomic assembly sequence. It does this once per page of the range, after taking a global lock, for every node that has the mm's processors, except the local node which uses the processor's own global purge instruction instead. Entry 0 is the control word and entry 1 the address word. After a batch of nodes it waits on the PIO write status.

struct.name: INT_CMP
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: Compare values for RTC comparators 1, 2 and 3 (header names SH_INT_CMPB, SH_INT_CMPC, SH_INT_CMPD; the header titles them 'RTC compare value for processor B, C, D'). The interrupt fires when the clock reaches the value. The comparator for RTC 0 would sit 0x80 below these and is not defined in the header (unknown).

struct.name: RTC
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: Real-time clock: a 55-bit counter, read by the kernel as its clock source (clock source rating 450, mask 55 bits) and for microsecond delays, because the CPU cycle counters are not synchronised across processors. The frequency is not in a register; the kernel asks firmware for it. The driver comment says the clock registers sit alone on a 64 KiB page, which is what lets user space map it read-only. The SHub 1 PROM (SAL 5.04) writes 0 to it at the SAL_B reset entry (0xffa94d20) and again to a node's counter in the interconnect phase, then reads it on every delay and timeout, so it must advance. Its tick period comes from rtc_ctl (SHub 1: 10 ns times the field plus one, 50 ns after the PROM's own write). See prom-reset.md.

struct.name: LB_ELECT
struct.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffc4e9b0, 0xffc4e766 (election reads), 0xffc4e246, 0xffa0b0f0 (bit updates); no Linux v5.3 name
struct.doc: Node election word; the name is ours. SAL_A stores slice + 1 to lb_elect_set and reads this register: the 64-bit value must equal exactly what was written, twice (site 0xffc4e9b0 and 0xffc4e766). Equal means this processor is the node's winner. Later code ORs bits 39 to 41 into it (set bit 41 when no other processor position is flagged; bit 40 set across nodes; bit 39 on a remote node) as firmware state. The relation to lb_elect_set is unknown: a write to the offset 8 above may alias, latch (first writer wins) or store into this word; the code reads the same register for all three.

struct.name: LB_ELECT_SET
struct.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffc4e9a6 (release store of slice + 1); no Linux v5.3 name
struct.doc: Election write register; the name is ours. SAL_A stores slice + 1 here and reads lb_elect. Whether it aliases lb_elect, latches the first writer or something else is unknown. A model that returns the written value at lb_elect satisfies every access read.

struct.name: LB_L1_STATE
struct.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffc4e790 and 0xffc4e7a0 (read-modify-write); the PROM's runtime also names the word sc_shub_state_reg and sc_shub_pushed_data_reg
struct.doc: L1 link state word in the local block; the name is ours. SAL_A's election winner sets bits 41:39 to 7 by read-modify-write, keeping the other bits. An earlier reading says the L1 start checks bits 41:39 for 7; a later review found no reader that does, so that requirement is unconfirmed and plain storage satisfies the write. Other bits are used by the L1 transport and are not decoded here.

field.name: link
field.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffc4e7a0 (write 7) ; the L1 start check named in boot-sequence.md is unconfirmed

struct.name: LB_LOCK
struct.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffa0ed30 (take), 0xffa0ee40 (release), 0xffa0e730 (user)
struct.doc: Firmware lock pair, release side; the name is ours. The PROM takes the lock by polling lb_lock_status until it reads 0, does a read-modify-write of cpu_bits, then writes 0 here. If the status does not read 0 within 1,000,000 microseconds it writes 0 here and polls again. Whether a read of lb_lock_status takes the lock in hardware is unknown; a plain register pair where the status always reads 0 satisfies every access read. Linux v5.3 does not define the lock; the PROM behaviour above is as observed at the access and the meaning is inferred.

struct.name: LB_LOCK_STATUS
struct.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffa0ed30 (the poll); the offset-form variant site 0xffa0e880 reads 0x1101d0208 on a remote node
struct.doc: Firmware lock status; the name is ours. The PROM polls it with a short delay until it reads 0; any non-zero value keeps it waiting until the 1,000,000 microsecond deadline, then it writes 0 to lb_lock and keeps polling, so a status that never reads 0 hangs the PROM. A read side effect is unknown. Linux v5.3 does not define the lock; the PROM behaviour above is as observed at the access and the meaning is inferred.

struct.name: PI_REG_2001_0100
struct.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffc4e800 and 0xffc4e816 (read-modify-write); Linux v5.3 defines no name
struct.doc: Processor interface register, unnamed (the block is inferred from the neighbouring SH1_PI_CAM_CONTROL and SH1_PIO_WRITE_STATUS_0); the name is ours. SAL_A reads it and writes it back with bit 24 set, using the read value for nothing else. The PROM later brackets writes to the register site 0x120000000 with bit 24 set then cleared, which suggests a write enable (inferred). Any reset value is tolerated; bit 24 must be settable and read back as written.

struct.name: PI_SLICE_PRESENT
struct.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffa115ac (read through the global window of the node), 0xffa99e2c (caller)
struct.doc: Per-slice flags in the processor interface; the name is ours. The local-master arbitration reads it for slices 0 and 1 other than the running one and tests bit slice; a set bit makes the PROM count that processor present and wait for it (up to 5,000,000 microseconds). On a one-processor node the bit for every other slice must read 0. The meaning (processor present) is inferred from that use. Later CPU-enumeration callers of the same word read bits 0 and 1 (first processor of slices 0 and 1) and bits 4 and 5 (second processor); the own-slice bit they expect was not traced, so a model should set it.

struct.name: PI_CAM_CONTROL
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: Control of CRB CAM access (header title; processor interface, inferred). The only use is a SHub 1.1 workaround: on a chip of revision 2 or lower the kernel writes 0x8000000000000010 here on every timer tick, through the address of its own node. What the value does is unknown.

struct.name: PIO_WRITE_STATUS
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: PIO write status, one per processor slice (header: PIO write status for CPU 0 and 1; processor interface, inferred). The kernel's memory-mapped-I/O write barrier spins until the pending write count shows idle. The kernel stores the address of the instance for its slice (the slice is the processor's position within the node) in its per-processor data.

struct.name: PIO_WRITE_STATUS_ALIAS
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: Alias of the PIO write status. The header names only the instance for slice 0. The deadlock recovery assembly adds 8 to whichever status address it was given, so the alias for slice 1 is inferred. Writing 7 clears the deadlock, write error and multiple write error bits (assembly comment); the header names only bit 1 (deadlock), so which of bits 0 and 2 is which is unknown. The kernel does this on SHub 1 and reads the alias instead on SHub 2.

struct.name: CPU_HIST
struct.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffc4e5c6 and 0xffc4e5e0 (progress write), 0xffa0ddb0; no Linux v5.3 name
struct.doc: Progress history of processor slice n (n = cr.lid bits 26:23, 0 to 3), 16 bytes apart; the name is ours. Every progress code is written as: read the word, shift it left 8, put the code in the low byte, write it back. The code is never read for a decision; any reset value is tolerated and the register must return what was last written. SAL_A also reads slice 1 and slice 3 words (0x150031510, 0x150031530) and copies them, ORed with 0x60, to LED registers. The block is the network interface's by address; the PROM uses it as plain storage (inferred).

struct.name: FW_WORD_1540
struct.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffc4ea06 (zeroed by the election winner); no Linux v5.3 name
struct.doc: Firmware scratch word; the name is ours. SAL_A's election winner writes 0 to it. No read was found in the reset phase. Plain storage satisfies the access.

struct.name: CPU_BITS
struct.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffc4ea00 (zeroed), 0xffa0e730 (set and clear a bit under the lock), 0xffa1d430 (test), 0xffa99cf0 and 0xffa9a130 (arbitration); no Linux v5.3 name
struct.doc: Firmware per-processor state word; the name is ours. The winner of the SAL_A election zeroes it. Bits the PROM uses: 21 + slice (tested in 0xffa1d430, set in the SAL_B reset entry), 26 + slice (set by the local-master arbitration, polled until the other present processors have set theirs), 30 + slice and bit 34 (a second barrier), 35 + slice (set in the SAL_B reset entry), and a 3-bit count at bit 47 (even slice) or bit 50 (odd slice) that each present slice publishes from a PAL call and the master waits for as that many ready bits among 29:26 (inferred). Bits are set and cleared by read-modify-write under the lock pair lb_lock and lb_lock_status. The SAL_A error path clears bits 29:26. The meanings are inferred from use; the word must read back what was written.

struct.name: FW_DEBUG_WORD
struct.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffc4ea10 (zeroed in SAL_A), 0xffa19e50 (loaded from the L1 reply in phase 0xe), 0xffa975e0 (bit test)
struct.doc: Firmware debug-switch word; the name is ours. SAL_A's election winner zeroes it; the PROM later stores the L1's reply to request 0x0001 and tests bits of it (bit 11 selects the single-node route, bit 14 skips I/O initialisation). Plain storage.

struct.name: JUNK_BUS_LED
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: Junk bus LED registers, one per processor slice (header SH1_REAL_JUNK_BUS_LED0 to 3, 64 KiB apart). The kernel keeps an 8-bit LED state per processor and stores it with a 16-bit write at LED0 plus slice times 64 KiB: bit 0 is the heartbeat, toggled twice a second from the timer interrupt, bit 1 an activity flag. The junk bus also holds the UART whose interrupt is event_occurred bit 20.
